video_title: Kalshi Cooked, Bitget Hacked + Agentic Bank Runs - The Chopping Block
gist: Chopping Block panel (Dragonfly, Gauntlet, Superstate) covers the ~$387M Lazarus hack of Bitget and the cross-chain censorship debate (THORChain vs NEAR Intents' Shield), the Consensys validator compromise as a challenge to ETH staking as a 'risk-free rate' (benchmarked against 35 bps US CDS), Kalshi's perps volume exposed as wash-like (~$3M OI vs hundreds of millions volume) leading to a CFTC probe, and Apollo's 'agentic bank runs' thesis that AI agents will erode deposit stickiness and consumer-laziness business models.

themes.theme: Bitget $387M hack and DPRK laundering routes

insights.claim: Bitget, a top-five exchange by derivatives volume, lost about $387 million mostly from hot/warm wallets in an infrastructure-linked hack very likely attributable to North Korea's Lazarus Group.
insights.speaker: host (Dragonfly partner)
insights.so_what: Exchange hot-wallet infrastructure remains the dominant attack surface for state-level hackers.

insights.claim: Bitget had a roughly $460 million insurance/user protection fund, enough to cover all claims, withdrawals have resumed, and the loss is smaller than its prior-year profit, so no contagion is expected.
insights.speaker: host (Dragonfly partner)
insights.so_what: Large CEX user-protection funds can absorb nine-figure hacks without solvency or contagion risk.
insights.quote: They had 460 million set aside in a insurance fund/user protection fund. So, that was enough to fully pay out all the claims.

insights.claim: The DPRK playbook after the hack was to dump freezable stablecoins first and move assets onto Ethereum and off chains like Arbitrum that have previously frozen hacked funds, since USDC freezes typically need a court order or law-enforcement instruction and take at least six hours.
insights.speaker: host (Dragonfly partner)
insights.so_what: Freezability is now a priced attribute that determines which assets and chains attackers flee first.

insights.claim: THORChain volume spikes during almost every major hack because it lets anyone swap cross-chain without screening, drawing accusations of 'decentralization theater' given its small validator set and history of shutting down after its own hack.
insights.speaker: host (Dragonfly partner)
insights.so_what: THORChain faces mounting regulatory and reputational risk as the go-to laundering rail.

insights.claim: NEAR Intents runs a validator-layer system called Shield that detects anomalies and hack reports; in this incident it froze about $500K and refused to route over $100 million of attacker funds.
insights.speaker: host (Dragonfly partner)
insights.so_what: NEAR is differentiating its cross-chain intents product on compliance-friendly screening, potentially attracting institutional flow.

insights.claim: NEAR's model is viewed as the best balance of being largely decentralized while censoring clearly illicit assets, as long as fully decentralized alternatives still exist at a worse cost (thinner liquidity, harder to move size).
insights.speaker: Tarun (Gauntlet)
insights.so_what: Pragmatic, screened decentralization may win cross-chain market share over 'free-for-all' protocols.

insights.claim: The cross-chain setting is where censorship fights concentrate because intents involve solvers, RFQs and someone signing messages across two systems of record, unlike a single-chain AMM where LPs have no control over who trades.
insights.speaker: Tarun (Gauntlet)
insights.so_what: Solver/relayer operators in cross-chain intents carry legal exposure that pure on-chain AMM LPs do not.

themes.theme: Censorship spectrum and chain-level property rights

insights.claim: One framing holds that infrastructure should sit at one of two extremes, fully neutral and censorship-resistant like the internet, or deliberately and systematically screening transactions, and that discretionary middle-ground interventions decided by a few humans serve nobody.
insights.speaker: Robert (Superstate)
insights.so_what: Protocols with ad hoc intervention policies may face both regulatory and credibility risk.
insights.quote: I think the middle ground doesn't work and is in nobody's favor.

insights.claim: Ethereum L1 is cited as the clear 'cannot shut down' extreme, which is why illicit funds historically used Tornado Cash on Ethereum.
insights.speaker: Robert (Superstate)
insights.so_what: Ethereum's credible neutrality is a structural moat for value that must not be censored.

insights.claim: A counterview argues fuller property rights mean not every valid state transition is legitimate, and AI-driven anomaly detection can programmatically flag stolen funds (e.g., assets sitting in a protocol ten minutes ago now in an attacker's balance) without abandoning neutrality.
insights.speaker: host (Dragonfly partner)
insights.so_what: Programmatic, AI-based theft detection could become a standard protocol-layer feature.

insights.claim: Chains act as 'laboratories of democracy' and users will increasingly choose chains based on their commitment to intervention and property-rights enforcement, much as depositors prefer countries that bail out their banks.
insights.speaker: host (Dragonfly partner)
insights.so_what: Intervention policy may become a competitive feature that drives liquidity between L2s.

insights.claim: Community values have shifted: Arbitrum's recent seizure of stolen funds was broadly accepted, whereas the same move in 2022-2023 post-FTX would likely have met much more hostility.
insights.speaker: host (Dragonfly partner)
insights.so_what: Crypto's tolerance for interventions is rising, lowering governance risk for chains that freeze hacked funds.

insights.claim: The optimal user point is estimated at roughly 80% of the way toward protection: a non-KYC, low-friction chain that still offers very high protection, since full protection becomes paternalistic like Coinbase account freezes.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: There is product room for low-friction chains that still credibly protect users from theft.

insights.claim: Tarun proposes that the market should be studied for implied premia across chains and privacy pools to infer whether users price chain security as a spectrum or a binary, arguing there have now been enough attacks to measure it.
insights.speaker: Tarun (Gauntlet)
insights.so_what: Cross-venue price spreads after hacks are an untapped dataset for pricing chain risk.

insights.claim: Same-asset price differences across chains (e.g., USDC on Arbitrum vs Ethereum vs a privacy protocol) stay tiny because they can be arbitraged within an hour, though distressed sellers of shielded assets would not realize par, similar to SVB's held-at-cost bonds.
insights.speaker: Robert (Superstate)
insights.so_what: Quoted parity hides liquidity discounts that only appear in forced selling.

insights.claim: Tokenized stocks issued on different chains should trade at small spreads driven by convenience rather than security, analogous to ADRs trading at premiums mainly for ease of access.
insights.speaker: Robert (Superstate)
insights.so_what: Relevant for tokenization issuers like Superstate: multi-chain fragmentation should not create large basis.

insights.claim: DAI has spiked to around $1.25 in the past for about ten minutes when a hacker dumped a large stack into it to escape freezable stablecoins.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Censorship-resistant stablecoins can see brief hack-driven squeezes.

themes.theme: Consensys validator hack and the 'risk-free' staking rate

insights.claim: Consensys's Ethereum staking validators were hacked; about 5% of Lido stake is delegated to Consensys validators, which mass-exited stake to rotate keys, with less than 1 ETH of unclaimed rewards taken and up to roughly 200 ETH in foregone rewards.
insights.speaker: host (Dragonfly partner)
insights.so_what: Validator-operator compromise is a real but so far small-loss risk vector for LST holders.

insights.claim: Because no principal was lost and no slashing occurred, the hit is opportunity cost, but it still impugns the idea of ETH staking as a 'risk-free rate', which is really the best possible rate rather than a floor.
insights.speaker: Robert (Superstate)
insights.so_what: Staking yield should carry a risk premium in DeFi pricing and looping strategies.
insights.quote: I think we think of staking as the risk-free rate, but it's really the best possible rate, not the worst possible rate

insights.claim: US sovereign CDS trades at about 35 basis points, implying the truly insured risk-free rate is roughly 35 bps below Treasury yields.
insights.speaker: host (Dragonfly partner)
insights.so_what: Gives a benchmark for pricing staking risk premia relative to sovereign risk.

insights.claim: A back-of-envelope estimate (5% chance per year of losing roughly two weeks of rewards) implies about one basis point of expected cost for Ethereum stakers, far below US CDS.
insights.speaker: host (Dragonfly partner)
insights.so_what: Current incidents imply negligible expected loss, so staking premia should stay small absent slashing.

insights.claim: Frontier AI models are expected to expose many more protocol and validator vulnerabilities, moving crypto from roughly zero observed validator risk into nonzero territory.
insights.speaker: Robert (Superstate)
insights.so_what: AI-driven exploit discovery raises tail risk across staking and DeFi, worth pricing in.
insights.quote: I think we've had roughly zero risks and now we're in the nonzero territory.

insights.claim: A finger-in-the-wind estimate puts the fair risk premium for Ethereum validation at about five basis points, well below US sovereign CDS.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Offers a rough anchor for staking insurance pricing.

insights.claim: Adding even a modest required risk premium to staking would reduce staking participation and especially ETH looping, and losing a month or year of rewards could force loopers to delever.
insights.speaker: host (Dragonfly partner)
insights.so_what: Leveraged LST loops are the most sensitive to validator-incident risk.
insights.quote: we definitely get less people looping.

insights.claim: Staking providers like Consensys could sell a fixed staking yield below market (e.g., guaranteed 3%) and absorb validator risk, effectively a total return swap on staking cash flows, which is easier to settle than a CDS.
insights.speaker: host (Dragonfly partner)
insights.so_what: Fixed-rate staking and staking insurance is a plausible new product line for large validators and DATs.

insights.claim: Ethereum's community is seen as caring disproportionately about stakers, so a catastrophic unfair slashing event would likely be rolled back at the beacon chain level, though not mere opportunity-cost losses.
insights.speaker: Tarun (Gauntlet)
insights.so_what: Implicit social backstop lowers tail risk of ETH staking principal.

insights.claim: A Swiss quant named Benny published a thread showing Kalshi's perpetual futures volume was massively inflated, with roughly $3 million of open interest against hundreds of millions of dollars of daily volume and repeated identical $5,500 lots traded back and forth in public order books.
insights.speaker: host (Dragonfly partner)
insights.so_what: Headline exchange volume on new perps venues can be largely fabricated; check OI-to-volume ratios.

insights.claim: The Wall Street Journal reported the CFTC is investigating Kalshi's volume claims, and Kalshi subsequently ended its liquidity incentive program, which should sharply cut its perps volume.
insights.speaker: host (Dragonfly partner)
insights.so_what: Regulatory scrutiny threatens Kalshi's growth narrative ahead of a targeted IPO.

insights.claim: Kalshi's maker rebate (about 0.3 bps to makers, 0.3 bps paid by takers) netted to zero, but certain market makers were reportedly earning equity based on volume, creating incentives to cross trades with each other.
insights.speaker: host (Dragonfly partner)
insights.so_what: Equity-for-volume deals are the same failure mode as token-incentivized perp DEX farming.

insights.claim: Pro-rata fixed-pie market maker incentives copied from venues like CME break down when only one or two makers compete, letting them implicitly collude to maximize their share.
insights.speaker: Tarun (Gauntlet)
insights.so_what: Incentive design must match market-maker competition depth or it invites wash trading.

insights.claim: Anyone inside Kalshi with dashboard access must have known the numbers were implausible, since with 3 million of open interest and 500 million of volume nobody but market makers was trading, making 98% of volume effectively fake.
insights.speaker: host (Dragonfly partner)
insights.so_what: Raises governance and disclosure concerns for a roughly $40 billion company marketing volume pre-IPO.
insights.quote: The most junior analyst inside the company looking at whatever graphana they had would have been like, "Hey, this looks cooked."

insights.claim: Coinbase International likewise shows high volume relative to very small open interest, signaling heavy market-maker incentives rather than organic activity.
insights.speaker: host (Dragonfly partner)
insights.so_what: Volume/OI ratio is a quick diagnostic for incentive-driven, non-organic exchange activity.

insights.claim: Kalshi paying for sponsored posts touting its perps volume was a red flag, since genuinely liquid exchanges market lower fees rather than volume, possibly reflecting pre-marketing ahead of a targeted IPO next year.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Paid volume marketing is a signal of weak organic traction.

insights.claim: Some long-tail Kalshi prediction markets with maker incentives (the ones it loses to Polymarket, such as political markets) also showed suspicious trading, though it is harder to prove than in perps.
insights.speaker: Tarun (Gauntlet)
insights.so_what: Inflated activity may extend beyond perps into Kalshi's core prediction markets.

themes.theme: Agentic bank runs and the end of consumer-laziness business models

insights.claim: An Apollo slide argues AI agents could cause 'agentic bank runs' by automatically sweeping idle checking balances into Treasuries and back as needed, eliminating the deposit stickiness that bank profitability relies on.
insights.speaker: host (Dragonfly partner)
insights.so_what: Bank net interest margins depend on lazy deposits that AI agents could optimize away.

insights.claim: Large banks pay about one basis point on checking deposits, and after ZIRP in 2008 deposit rates never bounced back, showing how extraordinarily sticky deposits are.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Deposit stickiness underpins bank NIM; any tech that breaks it is a structural threat.

insights.claim: Banks' Clarity Act argument that stablecoins will drain deposits is dismissed, since neobanks like Mercury and Column already offer better terms without causing mass exodus.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Stablecoin deposit-flight fears used in lobbying are likely overstated.

insights.claim: The shift to agent-managed money will be gradual rather than run-like because older Americans will be slow to hand financial control to agents, with intergenerational wealth transfer driving incremental adoption.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Expect a slow tectonic squeeze on bank deposits rather than a sudden shock.
insights.quote: This is going to be a very gradual tectonic shift.

insights.claim: New-generation banks like Column, Mercury and Erebor offer MCP hooks and APIs with fine-grained agent permissions, while JPMorgan will resist agent access as it fought even read-only Plaid access for a decade.
insights.speaker: host (Dragonfly partner)
insights.so_what: Agent-ready neobanks may capture deposits from incumbents that block API access.

insights.claim: Amazon blocked the Muse agent from shopping because most of its margin comes from sponsored search placement, which agents bypass, whereas DoorDash is pivoting to be agent-friendly since its revenue is fulfillment fees.
insights.speaker: host (Dragonfly partner)
insights.so_what: AI agents threaten ad-dependent marketplace models more than fee-based fulfillment models.

insights.claim: Hedge funds are discussing short baskets of companies relying on consumer laziness, such as hard-to-cancel subscriptions, expecting agents to cancel them; AOL still collects dial-up subscriptions from the 1990s.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Subscription and inertia-driven businesses are emerging short candidates in an agentic world.

insights.claim: Using the Muse agent on 10 years of health insurance records surfaced about $1,700 of dental and doctor overcharges, with about $200 recovered so far via agent-filed claims.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Insurance and billing, built on consumer inertia, are exposed to agent-driven claims recovery.

insights.claim: Agentic finance will make TradFi look like DeFi, where loopers already migrate instantly on 10 bps rate changes, turning the economy into a multi-trillion-dollar hot ball of money, and agents' homogeneity means more crowded, SVB-style fast runs.
insights.speaker: Tarun (Gauntlet)
insights.so_what: Crypto market dynamics are a leading indicator for how agent-driven TradFi flows will behave.
insights.quote: Instead of like a $10 billion hot ball of money, it's a $3 trillion hot ball of money that just moves around.

insights.claim: Compound v1 still holds millions of dollars despite a $30 million peak TVL, illustrating stranded or lost-key capital that agents will not move.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Not all capital is mobile; dormant balances persist even in DeFi.
